result.summary: Brennus's Gauls march on Delphi, where the Greeks hold them off and the god sends storms, rockfalls and a night panic. The Celts are routed, Brennus kills himself, and the remnants are harried out of Greece.

scenes.title: Greeks gather at Delphi
scenes.summary: Brennus marches on Delphi. The god promises protection and the Greek allies assemble, while the Aetolians harass Acichorius's division.
scenes.stakes: Delphi and its people face destruction by the invading Gauls.

scenes.title: Storm and battle at Delphi
scenes.summary: Earthquake, thunder, lightning, heroes' apparitions and falling crags torment the Celts. The Greeks attack at dawn and Brennus is wounded, forcing a retreat.
scenes.stakes: The Gauls risk annihilation; the Greeks risk losing the sanctuary.

scenes.title: Night panic of the Gauls
scenes.summary: Fleeing Gauls are seized by a panic and slaughter one another. Phocians guard their cattle, causing starvation.
scenes.stakes: The Gaulish army faces destruction from panic and hunger.

scenes.title: Pursuit and end of Brennus
scenes.summary: Athenians and Boeotians harry the stragglers, Brennus commits suicide, and the remnants are destroyed at the Sperchius. The Celts later cross back to Asia.
scenes.stakes: The retreating Gauls are being destroyed; Brennus faces shame.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses Galati and Celts for the same invading people.

notable_quotes.reason: The god's reassurance that he will protect his own sets up the miraculous defence.
Pausanias's brief assertion of the truthfulness of his account.

analysis.text: Divine protection of Delphi: nature and heroes fight for Apollo, and panic is called sent by the god.
The account reflects the Gallic invasion of Greece in 279 BC, which Greeks remembered as a miraculous deliverance of Delphi.

legacy.text: The word panic, from the god Pan, is explained here as fear without solid cause, and the repulse of the Gauls became a celebrated Delphic tradition.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias dates the event by the Athenian Archon and Olympiad, corresponding to 279/278 BC.

language_notes.text: Brennus led the Gallic (Celtic) invasion of Greece in 279 BC, the event Pausanias is narrating here.
"Flower of the army" means its best, most select troops.
Galati is Pausanias' name for the Gauls, the same people he also calls Celts.
Hyperochus, Laodocus, Pyrrhus (Neoptolemus) and Phylacus were local heroes, believed to defend Delphi in time of danger.
"Shot at them with perfect security" means the Phocians fired from the heights without risk of reprisal.
"Panic fear" derives from the god Pan, who was thought to cause sudden groundless terror; Pausanias glosses it as fear without solid cause.
"Bivouacked" means camped in the open without tents or shelter.
"Corn" here means grain generally, not maize.
"Neat wine" means wine undiluted with water; Greeks normally mixed wine with water, so drinking it freely was extreme.
Dating by the Athenian Archon and the Olympiad was the standard Greek way of naming a year.

context_notes.text: The oracle of Apollo at Delphi was the most famous in Greece; its priests spoke for the god.
Heraclea, near Thermopylae, was the Gallic base where Acichorius guarded the treasure and baggage.
Parnassus is the mountain above Delphi, sacred to Apollo and the Muses.
Galati and Celts are names for the same Gallic invaders, who attacked Greece in 279 BC under Brennus.
Heraclea was a town near Thermopylae, in the region where the Gauls had earlier camped.
The Sperchius is a river in southern Thessaly flowing into the Malian Gulf; the Malienses lived around it.
Some Gauls, called Galatians, settled in central Asia Minor in a region later named Galatia.

literary_notes.text: The narrator states the god's enmity outright, framing the following natural disasters as divine intervention.
Rising numbers of dead from a single crag, with crags seeming to aim at the Celts, heighten the sense of divine wrath.
The bravest bodyguard fights on, yet one wound to Brennus breaks the army, and they kill their own helpless comrades.
The Gauls destroy themselves, each mistaking friends for Greek enemies, so the invaders do the Greeks' killing for them.
Pausanias attributes the panic to the god, showing his belief in divine intervention protecting Delphi.
Brennus's suicide from shame shows him as a leader overwhelmed by responsibility for the disaster, ending his story bleakly.
The abrupt claim of truthfulness asserts the historian's authority and closes the account plainly.
